newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO names time and place of enlargement summit.
newsitem.headline: NATO names time and place of enlargement summit.

text.p: NATO on Tuesday called a special summit in Madrid on July 8-9 to name its first new members from former communist Europe, but sought to deflect Russian anger by pledging not to station nuclear weapons on their territory.

NATO foreign ministers also agreed to send a new peace force to Bosnia for 18 months and lambasted Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic for failing to respect the results of November's municipal elections.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana told reporters leaders of the 16-member alliance would gather at a special summit in the Spanish captial to invite certain countries to begin accession talks.
They will be the first new members for more than 2-1/2 decades. The goal is for them to win membership in time for the alliance's 50th anniversary in 1999.
Solana said the summit would "set the course for the alliance as it moves towards the 21st century, consolidating Euro-Atlantic security".

He said that in parallel with moves to expand the alliance eastwards, NATO also hoped to reach an agreement with Russia "at the earliest possible date on the development of a strong, stable and enduring security partnership".
Reading from a final communique of the meeting, Solana said the alliance had no plans to station nuclear weapons on the territory of new members.

"Enlarging the Alliance will not require a change in NATO's current nuclear posture... NATO countries have no intention, no plan, and no reason to deploy nuclear weapons on the territory of new members," Solana said.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said the ministers had authorised Solana to open negotiations with Russia on a possible charter embracing all aspects of relations between the two former foes.
"The door is open, Russia should walk through it," he told a press conference, adding a deal would be both for the good of Russia and for "the good of Europe."

But there was little indication the offer on nuclear weapons, which are no longer deployed on the western European mainland, would change Russia's view against enlargement and there were no other inducements to try and coax it into talks.

Shortly before Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov left Moscow to attend the second day of the two-day Brussels meeting, Russia dismissed suggestions it was softening its opposition as "fantasy".
NATO officials stressed that Russia had agreed to take part in a Stabilisation Force (SFOR) taking over from the alliance's current peace-keeping contingent in Bosnia on December 20.
"We hope we can build on that cooperation on the ground to convince them enlargement is no threat," a NATO envoy said.
"We realise they are in a difficult position, they cannot appear to accept that enlargement is going ahead," he added.
The ministers agreed to send between 25,000 and 30,000 troops to monitor the Balkan state's peace accords next year, but said the force would leave at the end of 18 months.
NATO, which has spent the last year policing the Dayton peace accords on Bosnia, "strongly deplored" Milosevic's cancellation of local election results in Serbia last month.
A NATO statement issued shortly after the start of the meeting also praised the restraint of the Serbian opposition, which has mounted peaceful mass protests against the decision.
Christopher added that there was no place in the new Europe "for an unreformed dictatorship that refuses to heed the will of its people."
